Mexico.name: Mexico
Mexico.territory_label_en: Federal system — 3 tiers: federation, 32 states, and municipalities
Mexico.constitution_current: Political Constitution of the United Mexican States (CPEUM), as amended to 2026
Mexico.intl_law_incorporation: Constitutional bloc via the pro-persona principle
Mexico.intl_law_article: Art. 1 CPEUM (2011 reform): all persons enjoy the human rights recognised in this Constitution and in international human rights treaties; norms shall be interpreted so as to afford the broadest protection to persons.
Mexico.intl_law_note: The 2011 constitutional reform elevated human rights treaties to constitutional rank via the constitutional bloc (bloque de constitucionalidad). SCJN Contradicción de Tesis 293/2011: express constitutional restrictions in the text of the CPEUM prevail over treaties; however, the pro-persona principle applies in zones of silence.
Mexico.treaty_hierarchy: Human rights treaties at constitutional level via the constitutional bloc; other treaties above federal laws but below the Constitution (Art. 133 CPEUM)
Mexico.constitutional_review: Amparo (individual) + Acción de Inconstitucionalidad (abstract) + Controversia Constitucional
Mexico.federal_complication: 32 states each enact their own electoral codes for local elections. Federal electoral law (LGIPE, LGPP) covers federal offices only. Rights may be unequally guaranteed at state and municipal level.
key_structural_features: Pro-persona principle (Art. 1 CPEUM) requires the broadest possible interpretation of rights
SCJN control de convencionalidad: judges must apply the American Convention on Human Rights (ACHR) directly
TEPJF has binding jurisprudential criteria on electoral rights
INE (Art. 41 CPEUM): constitutionally autonomous electoral authority organising federal elections
OPLEs: state-level electoral bodies for local elections, coordinated by INE on federal matters
Electoral amparo: limited scope; TEPJF holds jurisdiction over most electoral rights challenges

constitutional_pyramid.label: Constitutional Bloc
instruments: CPEUM + Human Rights Treaties (Art. 1 CPEUM, 2011 reform)
constitutional_pyramid.note: Human rights treaties elevated to constitutional rank. Express CPEUM restrictions prevail (CT 293/2011).

constitutional_pyramid.label: Organic / General Electoral Laws
instruments: Ley Federal de Revocación de Mandato
constitutional_pyramid.note: Regulatory statutes for constitutional electoral provisions (Arts. 35, 41, 99 CPEUM).

constitutional_pyramid.label: Ordinary Federal Laws
instruments: Ley General de Acceso de las Mujeres a una Vida Libre de Violencia
Ley General para la Inclusión de Personas con Discapacidad
constitutional_pyramid.note: Ordinary laws intersecting with political rights on a cross-cutting basis.

constitutional_pyramid.label: INE Regulations and Agreements
constitutional_pyramid.note: Operational regulation; must conform to LGIPE and the CPEUM.

constitutional_pyramid.label: State Electoral Laws
constitutional_pyramid.note: Govern local elections. Must respect constitutional bases and the relevant provisions of LGIPE.

treaty_ratification.notes: First country in Latin America to ratify the CRPD. CRPD/C/MEX/CO/1 (2014).

key_tensions.label: Constitutional bloc v. express restrictions (CPEUM Art. 38)
key_tensions.description: Art. 1 CPEUM incorporates the CRPD into the constitutional bloc, but Art. 38 contains express restrictions on political rights. SCJN CT 293/2011 holds that express constitutional restrictions prevail over treaties. This creates a zone of tension: can Art. 38 suspend political rights even though CRPD Art. 29 prohibits restrictions based on legal capacity?

key_tensions.label: INE autonomy (Art. 41 CPEUM) v. popular election of councillors (2023 reform)
key_tensions.description: Art. 41 CPEUM establishes the constitutional autonomy of the INE. The 2023 reform (under debate) would introduce popular election of INE councillors. IACHR Advisory Opinion OC-28/21 holds that mechanisms for selecting electoral authorities must guarantee structural independence. Popular election may undermine that independence.

key_tensions.label: Federalism and unequal coverage of rights
key_tensions.description: Political participation rights are guaranteed unevenly across the 32 states. Recall of mandate exists only for the federal president (Art. 35 IX CPEUM). Independent candidacies exist at federal level but their regulation varies across states. ILO 169 was ratified at federal level but implementation varies by state.

Costa Rica.name: Costa Rica
Costa Rica.territory_label: Unitario centralizado (7 provincias, cantons, distritos — sin autonomía legislativa subnacional)
Costa Rica.territory_label_en: Centralised unitary state (7 provinces, cantons, districts — no subnational legislative autonomy)
Costa Rica.constitution_current: Political Constitution of Costa Rica (1949), as amended
Costa Rica.intl_law_incorporation: Expanded constitutional bloc via Sala IV jurisprudence
Costa Rica.intl_law_article: Art. 7 CN: international treaties have authority superior to laws. Sala IV (Voto 9469-2007 and subsequent jurisprudence): human rights treaties may rank equal to or above the Constitution where they afford greater protection to the individual.
Costa Rica.intl_law_note: Sala IV determines treaty hierarchy on a case-by-case basis. Pro-individuo approach: where a treaty affords greater protection than the Constitution, the treaty prevails. This is broader than the Mexican post-CT 293/2011 model.
Costa Rica.treaty_hierarchy: Human rights treaties at supra-constitutional level where they afford greater protection; other treaties above ordinary laws (Art. 7 CN)
Costa Rica.constitutional_review: Recurso de amparo + Acción de inconstitucionalidad before Sala IV (Sala Constitucional)
Costa Rica.review_body: Sala IV (Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court)
Costa Rica.federal_complication: Not applicable — centralised unitary system. Less normative fragmentation than Mexico. The gap is not between levels of government but between recognised rights and operative implementation mechanisms.
key_structural_features: TSE is the 4th Branch of State (Arts. 9, 99–104 CN): the sole supreme electoral authority
TSE electoral decisions are final and unappealable (Art. 103 CN) — tension with ACHR Art. 25
Sala IV: electoral amparo is theoretically available, but the TSE holds exclusive jurisdiction in electoral matters
No independent candidacies: only registered political parties may nominate candidates (Art. 98 CN)
Mandatory gender parity in candidacies (Art. 2, Electoral Code)

constitutional_pyramid.label: Constitutionality Bloc (Sala IV)
instruments: CN 1949 + Human Rights Treaties (when more favourable to the individual)
constitutional_pyramid.note: Sala IV may elevate treaties above the CN if they afford greater protection. More dynamic framework than the Mexican model.

constitutional_pyramid.label: Organic Laws (qualified majority)
instruments: Organic Law of the Civil Registry
constitutional_pyramid.note: Require 38 votes of the Asamblea Legislativa for approval or reform.

constitutional_pyramid.label: Electoral Code and Electoral Laws
constitutional_pyramid.note: Primary electoral framework. Approved by simple majority in the Asamblea.

constitutional_pyramid.label: Ordinary Laws
constitutional_pyramid.note: Cross-cutting laws affecting the political participation of specific groups.

constitutional_pyramid.label: TSE Regulations and Resolutions
constitutional_pyramid.note: Operational regulation. The TSE holds exclusive regulatory power in electoral matters.

treaty_ratification.notes: One of the first countries to ratify.
Seat of the IACHR in San José.
Ratified in 1993, but without specific electoral implementation.
Political endorsement; no electoral implementation mechanism.

key_tensions.label: TSE Art. 103 (finality) v. ACHR Art. 25 (effective remedy)
key_tensions.description: Art. 103 CN establishes that TSE resolutions in electoral matters are final and unappealable. ACHR Art. 25 guarantees an effective judicial remedy against violations of fundamental rights. If the TSE violates rights in an electoral decision, does an effective remedy exist? Sala IV has taken varying positions. The IACHR has not directly resolved this for Costa Rica, but the principle of access to justice requires at least one instance of independent review.

key_tensions.label: ACHR Art. 23 (participation) v. CN Arts. 96–98 (party monopoly)
key_tensions.description: ACHR Art. 23.1(b) guarantees the right to be elected in genuine elections. The IACHR in Castañeda Gutman v. Mexico (2008) held that where a party system is the only route to elective office, it may constitute a disproportionate restriction. CN Arts. 96–98 of Costa Rica prohibit independent candidacies: only registered political parties may nominate candidates. Costa Rica has not yet been subject to specific Inter-American litigation on this point.

key_tensions.label: ILO 169 Arts. 6–7 (indigenous consultation and participation) v. absence of electoral mechanism
key_tensions.description: ILO 169 (ratified 1993) obliges Costa Rica to establish mechanisms for consultation and political participation of indigenous peoples in matters affecting them. The Electoral Code does not include mechanisms for indigenous-specific electoral representation or participation. The Indigenous Law (CONAI) recognises indigenous governance structures but without connection to the formal electoral system.
